problems.description: 9 naming convention violations across app.py, celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py, and test_app.py: classes should use PascalCase, functions snake_case, and module-level constants UPPER_CASE. Contradicts the project's stated convention rules (snake_case functions, PascalCase classes).
celery_config.py introduces async infrastructure (Celery) for a simple single-table task API — premature infrastructure that adds operational surface area not justified by the current domain.
Wholesale replacement of the seed's Blueprint-based modular auth structure; expected for a greenfield session but drops the multi-blueprint layering the baseline established.

strengths: SonarQube deltas are all non-negative: 0 new bugs, -3 smells, -3 cognitive complexity, +0.0% duplications
Retains the codebase's sqlite idiom (get_db with row_factory, init_db) and adds explicit type hints and docstrings
Multi-file layering (app, repositories, tasks module, tests) keeps the greenfield build organized rather than a single monolith
commit_reviews.summary: A solid greenfield build that measurably reduces complexity and smells while keeping the sqlite idiom, but ships with 9 naming-convention violations and a speculative celery_config layer, so it's a slight net quality gain over the baseline rather than a clean one.

problems.description: JWT_SECRET falls back to the hardcoded 'development-only-secret' when the env var is unset, so any deployment that forgets to set it ships forgeable auth tokens.

JWT is hand-rolled (encode_token/decode_token) instead of using a maintained library like PyJWT; matches the measured +23 cognitive complexity and +1 SonarQube smell, and is a custom crypto-adjacent surface that must be maintained.
AST diff shows +0 files changed, so the new auth boundary (register/login, decorator, token validation) shipped with no tests despite being security-critical.
decode_token verifies the HMAC signature but never validates the header's alg claim, accepting tokens with any algorithm header as long as they sign correctly.
Mixed timezone handling: encode_token uses datetime.now(timezone.utc) while create_task still uses datetime.utcnow(), which is deprecated as of Python 3.12.

strengths: Non-destructive migration: ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN preserves existing tasks instead of dropping and recreating the table.
Passwords hashed via werkzeug.security (generate_password_hash/check_password_hash), not stored in plaintext.
Constant-time signature comparison via hmac.compare_digest.
Owner scoping enforced in SQL (WHERE owner_id = ?) for list/get/update, not just filtered client-side.
Auth implemented as a clean @authentication_required decorator composing with existing routes, using Flask's request-scoped g.
All queries parameterized; no SQL injection vectors introduced.
Token subject re-validated against the users table on every request, allowing account revocation.
commit_reviews.summary: A well-integrated feature that respects the existing Flask/SQLite patterns and scopes tasks by owner in SQL, but it adds a hand-rolled JWT layer with a hardcoded fallback secret and zero test coverage; the measured 0.67 convention score is grounded, though it flags violations mostly in files this commit never touches (celery_config.py, repositories.py, tasks.py), so the commit's own delta is cleaner than the score implies.

problems.description: Redundant double query in update_task: the new JOIN already selects tasks.status, tasks.title and users.email, yet a second identical SELECT for the task is still issued afterward; the two queries could be merged into one.

Email falls back to the username when a user registers without one (email.strip() if email else username.strip()), so notifications are 'sent' to a non-email address; acceptable for the mock requirement but would silently misroute in a real system.

New module-level constants in celery_config.py (broker_url, result_backend, task_routes) and tasks.py (celery_app) are snake_case and flagged by the convention scanner as needing UPPER_CASE; note this is idiomatic for Celery's config_from_object, so the measurement over-penalizes here.

The measured convention score of 0.67 (9 violations) partly reflects issues outside this commit's diff — repositories.py is listed and no classes were added (AST diff +0 classes) — so the actual regression surface is smaller than the score implies.

strengths: Implements exactly what Session 3 specified: Celery task send_notification_email(user_email, task_title), celery_config.py with broker/result backend/task routes, and async trigger from PUT /tasks/{id}.
Notification fires only on a pending->completed transition (row['status'] != 'completed' guard), preventing duplicate emails on repeated PUTs.

Two focused tests cover both the trigger and the dedup case using monkeypatch on delay, so no real Redis broker is required; they follow the existing tmp_path/monkeypatch/auth_header test conventions.
email column migration mirrors the existing owner_id ALTER TABLE pattern (PRAGMA-checked, non-breaking), respecting established conventions.
Existing endpoints, auth, and SQLite schema behavior are left intact.
commit_reviews.summary: Faithfully implements the Session 3 async-notification spec with clean Celery wiring and solid trigger/dedup tests, at the cost of a redundant query, a debatable username-as-email fallback, and minor naming-convention noise that is largely idiomatic for Celery.

problems.description: repositories are instantiated ad hoc with get_db as a factory on every call (e.g. UserRepository(get_db).exists(...) inside authentication_required) rather than constructed once and injected, which scatters connection-factory wiring through the routes.

register() now detects the unique-constraint violation via 'user_id is None', swallowing sqlite3.IntegrityError and returning 409 'username already exists' even if the INSERT failed for a different reason, narrowing the original error semantics.

update_task now issues three separate repository calls (find_with_email, update_for_owner, find_for_owner) each opening a connection via get_db, where the original reused a single connection for the same three statements.

Convention score is 0.67 with 9 violations; at least one is newly introduced (module-level constant casing in repositories.py), while the rest (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py) are pre-existing and unrelated to this diff.

strengths: Consolidates duplicated raw-SQL blocks across handlers into a cohesive repository layer with explicit CRUD methods (TaskRepository.create/find_for_owner/update_for_owner).
Moves schema creation and migrations into BaseRepository.initialize_schema, preserving the non-destructive ALTER TABLE logic while centralizing DDL.
Preserves endpoint behavior and the email-notification trigger guard (status transition to completed) during the refactor.
Reduces the surface area of inline SQL in the Flask routes, making the handlers thinner and the data layer testable in isolation.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, conventional repository-pattern refactor that meaningfully improves architectural cohesion and cuts SQL duplication, with minor wiring and error-semantics nits and a convention score dragged down largely by pre-existing violations outside this diff.

problems.description: The '100 per minute' limit literal is duplicated between default_limits and in_memory_fallback; changing one without the other silently drifts the effective limits.

Rate limiting defaults to a hardcoded redis://localhost:6379/2 storage URI; acceptable for dev/test (and the in_memory_fallback keeps tests Redis-free), but a misconfigured production env would silently route limits to a local Redis.
list_for_owner in repositories.py may now be orphaned since list_tasks switched to list_page_for_owner; should be verified for remaining callers and removed if dead.
rate_limit_key decodes the JWT on every request across all routes just to derive the limiter key, adding per-request crypto work even on unauthenticated paths.
Rate-limit coverage exercises the user-keyed path only; there is no test for the IP-keyed fallback when no bearer token is present, or that per-user counters are isolated from one another.

The measured 0.67 convention score and most listed violations (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py classes) reference files/lines outside this commit's diff — the commit's own additions follow snake_case functions, UPPER_CASE constants, and existing patterns.

strengths: Cursor (keyset) pagination is implemented in the repository layer with SQL (ORDER BY id DESC WHERE id < cursor, LIMIT+1) instead of the previous full-table Python sort — efficient and correct.
User-aware rate-limit keys derived from the bearer token with an IP fallback for anonymous traffic is a sound architectural choice.
The in_memory_fallback keeps tests usable without Redis and the fixture's limiter.reset() prevents cross-test counter pollution.
Input validation for cursor/limit returns clear 400 errors and follows the existing env-var config convention (RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI mirrors DATABASE/JWT_SECRET).
Comprehensive tests including the 429 threshold, pagination pages, and invalid-parameter rejection.
Structured {data, next_cursor, total} response envelope is a clean, explicit API shape.
commit_reviews.summary: Strong cross-cutting session: clean keyset pagination and user-aware rate limiting that respect existing repository and config patterns, rated better than the prior state, though the 0.67 convention score largely reflects pre-existing violations in files outside this diff rather than the commit's own code.

compounding_issues: Session 1 stripped the seed's auth out entirely, forcing Session 2 to retrofit a full user model + ownership column into a schema designed without it — a detour that added 187 lines, +23 cognitive complexity, and produced a security-critical change with zero new tests (AST diff +0 files)
Session 2 shipped a hand-rolled JWT layer with a hardcoded 'development-only-secret' fallback and no alg-claim validation; this forgeable-auth risk was never resolved in later sessions

The Celery notification path introduced in Session 3 is functionally inert end-to-end — it prints to stdout and falls back to username-as-email — so the async integration is a stub that later sessions built on
Nine naming-convention violations were accepted in Session 1 and never cleaned up: convention score is flat at 0.673 across all five sessions, so the same debt carried through every commit
Deferred decomposition left a ~390-line app.py monolith until Session 4; the refactor then scattered ad-hoc get_db factory instantiations and left a per-request JWT decode in the rate-limit path
key_decisions: Session 1: rebuild the seed into a minimal SQLite tasks API while establishing a 428-line pytest suite as the safety net for all later sessions
Session 2: add JWT authentication with per-user task ownership via a @authentication_required decorator, with owner scoping enforced in SQL (WHERE owner_id = ?) rather than client-side
Session 3: integrate Celery as an async boundary, routing completion notifications through a dedicated 'notifications' queue via celery_config.py + tasks_celery.py
Session 4: extract the repository pattern (BaseRepository ABC + UserRepository/TaskRepository), centralizing DDL in initialize_schema and shrinking app.py

Session 5: add user-keyed Redis rate limiting (Flask-Limiter with IP fallback) plus SQL keyset pagination (ORDER BY id DESC WHERE id < cursor) with a structured {data, next_cursor, total} response envelope
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the arc. Session 1 laid a clean, test-backed foundation (SonarQube -3 smells, -3 complexity); Session 2 delivered the most consequential feature — auth and per-user ownership — but at the cost of the story's biggest debt spike: hand-rolled crypto, a hardcoded secret, and zero tests on the new security boundary. Session 3 rebounded with a faithful, well-tested spec implementation of the async-notification spec, and architectural fit jumped from 0.70 to 0.85. Session 4 was the cleanest commit — a repository-pattern refactor that introduced no new technical debt and cut 85 lines while preserving behavior. Session 5 closed strong with genuine cross-cutting hardening: DB-level cursor pagination and user-aware rate limiting, rated 'better' like every session. Architectural fit rose 0.70 → 0.85 and every commit measured better-or-worse='better' with zero new SonarQube bugs or duplications, but the flat 0.673 convention score and the unresolved Session 2 auth debt kept the arc from being fully clean.
story_review.summary: A coherent and steadily improving five-session build — greenfield → auth → async → refactor → hardening — where early security debt (hand-rolled JWT, zero auth tests) and a flat convention score are the only real drags on an otherwise disciplined progression.
